title: Post-Course Portfolio: Study Group Web App
descriptionMarkdown:
# Study Group Web App

## Position in the curriculum

Post-course portfolio: build after finishing the full curriculum through the final capstone. This project's focus is many-to-many relationships (a member belongs to many groups; a group has many members) and date/time-driven scheduling logic, which none of the earlier, simpler catalog entries exercise.

## What is graded, and what is external

This project has a dedicated, automatically-graded checkpoint: **`session-overlap-checkpoint`** ("Session overlap scheduler"), a pure in-memory `SessionScheduler.run(String input)` program using `java.time.LocalDateTime` to implement exactly the overlap-detection and chronological-listing core. Passing its hidden tests proves your date/time reasoning is correct, independent of any real JPA mapping.

The real many-to-many relationship, a genuine JPA `@ManyToMany` (or an explicit join entity), and a rating feature, are external and self-reviewed.

## Architecture overview

```text
GroupController                 <- create group, join/leave, schedule session, upcoming
GroupService                     <- your checkpoint's overlap-detection rules, reshaped as a Spring bean
Member / StudyGroup (JPA entities)
Membership (join entity)          <- member, group, joinedAt — explicit, not a bare @ManyToMany, so it carries its own data
Session (JPA entity)              <- group, start, duration
SessionRating (JPA entity)        <- member, session, rating — UNIQUE (member, session)
```

## Build it as vertical slices

1. **Slice 1 — port the checkpoint logic into a service.** Carry your overlap-detection and upcoming-listing rules into `GroupService`, unit tests unchanged, with an injected `Clock` (never `LocalDateTime.now()` directly).
2. **Slice 2 — the many-to-many relationship.** Model `Membership` as an explicit join entity (not a bare `@ManyToMany`) so you can record `joinedAt`, and confirm both directions of the relationship (a member's groups; a group's members) stay correct after several joins and leaves.
3. **Slice 3 — real scheduling with the overlap check.** Wire the checkpoint's overlap logic into a real `POST /sessions` endpoint, returning a clear conflict response.
4. **Slice 4 — timezone-correct scheduling.** Accept and normalize sessions expressed in different offsets, confirming an overlap is detected correctly regardless of which zone each request used.
5. **Slice 5 — ratings with a database constraint.** Add `SessionRating` with a `UNIQUE (member, session)` constraint, and confirm a second rating attempt is rejected at the database level.

## Common pitfalls

- **Reading the system clock directly inside the "upcoming sessions" or overlap logic.** This makes date-dependent behavior untestable without waiting for real time to pass; inject a `Clock` everywhere, exactly as your checkpoint's tests already required.
- **Using a bare `@ManyToMany` when you actually need to record when a member joined.** An explicit join entity is required the moment the relationship itself carries data.
- **Normalizing time zones inconsistently between the write path and the overlap check.** Convert everything to a single reference (UTC `Instant`, or a consistently normalized `ZonedDateTime`) before comparing.
- **Relying only on an application-level check to prevent a duplicate rating.** Back it with a real `UNIQUE` constraint, exactly as Chapter 19's uniqueness lesson requires.

## How to self-test what the checkpoint cannot reach

- Join and leave a group several times and confirm, via a direct repository query, that the `Membership` history (not just current membership) is what you intended to keep or discard.
- Schedule two sessions for the same member expressed in two different UTC offsets that would overlap once normalized, and confirm the conflict is detected.
- Attempt to rate the same session twice as the same member and confirm the second attempt fails with a database constraint violation, not just an application check.

## Required evidence

- A many-to-many relationship test confirming a member's group list and a group's member list both stay correct after several joins and leaves.
- A scheduling-conflict test suite covering back-to-back sessions with no overlap (allowed), a genuine overlap (rejected), and sessions in different time zones normalized to the same instant before comparison.
- A database constraint (and a test) preventing a member from rating the same session twice.
- A `@DataJpaTest` for the "upcoming sessions across all groups" query, confirming correct chronological ordering and exclusion of past sessions relative to the injected clock.
- A migration adding the membership join table with its own timestamp column, applied through a versioned migration tool.

## Review and completion

A reviewer schedules two sessions in different groups that overlap for one shared member, in two different time zones expressed as ISO-8601 offsets, and expects the conflict to be detected correctly regardless of which zone each request was expressed in — then changes the injected clock to a specific instant and confirms the "upcoming sessions" list updates accordingly with no code change beyond the clock.
learningObjectives: Complete the graded session-overlap-scheduler checkpoint and carry its verified date/time logic into a real JPA-backed service
Model and query a many-to-many relationship through an explicit join entity carrying its own data
Detect a scheduling conflict correctly across time zones using an injected Clock, not the system clock
Enforce a one-rating-per-member-per-session rule with a database constraint, not application logic alone
Manage a join-table schema change through a versioned migration
